title: HTTP: Methods, Status Codes & Headers
summary: HTTP is the set of messages browsers and servers use to request and return web resources.

subtopics.title: Main idea
subtopics.explanation: A request includes a method, a URL, headers, and sometimes a body. The URL names the resource; headers add details; a body can carry submitted data. It is like a form sent to a service desk. The server responds with a status and may return content. Not every request needs a body. In practice, a browser can send GET for a page and POST for a submitted form. In practice, a browser may make an OPTIONS preflight before a cross-origin request.

subtopics.title: Important part
subtopics.explanation: GET usually asks to read a resource, such as a list of products. Repeating a GET should not normally change server state. It is like asking to see a menu. Do not use GET for actions that delete or purchase data, because links and caches may repeat or share the request. In practice, a request body can carry structured form data, while headers describe its format. In practice, a 401 generally asks for authentication, while a 403 indicates access is refused.

subtopics.title: How it works
subtopics.explanation: A status code summarizes the outcome. A 2xx response usually means success, 4xx points to a request or permission problem, and 5xx signals a server failure. It is like a receipt code telling you whether an order was accepted. Client code should handle expected outcomes instead of assuming every response succeeded. In practice, a 404 means the requested resource was not found; a 500 points to server trouble. In practice, a response can succeed at the transport level while its body represents a domain-level error.

subtopics.title: A useful detail
subtopics.explanation: Headers carry details such as content type, caching instructions, and authentication context. They are like labels attached to a package. A browser uses them to interpret the response and decide whether it can reuse a cached copy. Do not put secret values in places exposed to client-side JavaScript. In practice, a response content-type header helps the browser understand the returned data. In practice, cache headers influence whether a later request can reuse a response.

subtopics.title: Good practice
subtopics.explanation: HTTPS is HTTP carried through TLS encryption. It helps protect data while it travels between browser and server and helps verify the server identity. It is like sending a sealed package to the intended address. HTTPS does not make an application automatically secure; validate inputs and protect accounts as well. In practice, hTTPS protects the network connection, but the API still needs access checks. In practice, do not place credentials in a URL because URLs can be logged or shared.

foundations.overview: HTTP is the request-and-response system browsers use to talk with web servers. A request says what resource is needed and what action is intended; the response reports what happened and may include data. Think of it like ordering at a counter and receiving a status plus the item. Learn methods, status codes, and headers together, and use HTTPS for protected transport.
foundations.whyItMatters: HTTP defines how clients and servers exchange requests and responses. Reading its methods, statuses, headers, and security properties helps build resilient frontend flows.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser sets many headers automatically (Origin, Cookie, Accept) and enforces rules like CORS based on response headers.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Designing/consuming REST endpoints, setting Cache-Control, handling 401/403 auth flows, and diagnosing failed fetches.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct status codes and caching headers improve reliability, cacheability, and client behavior across the product.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Reading status codes and headers lets you fix the actual failure layer instead of guessing.
foundations.performanceImpact: Cache-Control, ETags, and compression headers cut bytes and round-trips; keep-alive and HTTP/2 reduce connection overhead.
commonUseCases: Consuming a REST API with fetch

commonMisconceptions.reality: 401 = not authenticated (who are you?); 403 = authenticated but not allowed (you can't do this).

commonMisconceptions.myth: A CORS error is a server being down.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's the browser blocking a cross-origin response that lacks the right Access-Control-* headers; the request often succeeded server-side.

keyTakeaways: A request includes a method, a URL, headers, and sometimes a body.
GET usually asks to read a resource, such as a list of products.
A status code summarizes the outcome.
Headers carry details such as content type, caching instructions, and authentication context.
HTTPS is HTTP carried through TLS encryption.
